newsitem.title: USA: Lead and zinc markets set to firm in 1997 - Comico.
newsitem.headline: Lead and zinc markets set to firm in 1997 - Comico.

text.p: Cominco's Red Dog mine, the world's biggest zinc orebody, may soon get to wag its tail and shake off the torpor which has plagued zinc prices for the past three years as the metal's value was virtually ignored by the base metals boom.

Zinc metal prices look set to firm up over the coming year as stocks fall to manageable levels, and lead prices will remain strongly underpinned, said Roger Brain, Cominco's vice-president of sales and marketing.

"The fundamentals of the zinc market continue to move in the right direction. Demand has finally caught up with supply," Brain said. "I believe zinc is going to have its day and some time next year we will see significantly higher prices."

The galvanized steel market will continue to grow, Brain said, with some 20 new continuous galvanizing lines to be built over the next two to three years, supporting a two percent annual demand growth.
Zinc stocks peaked at three times their normal level of five weeks' supply throughout the system back in 1994, and Brain expected stocks to fall to the five weeks level sometime in 1997.
Eastern bloc zinc exports will also slip from current levels, he said.

The zinc price has been trapped in the mid 40 cents a lb range for the past three to four years. "Most people don't make much money at this level," Brain said. "When stocks get down to more normal levels, we would like to see the price return to more normal levels of 55 to 60 cents per pound."
Brain expected global zinc stocks to shrink by 250,000 tonnes this year, with a further decline of the same order in 1997.

Refining capacity has been largely unchanged for several years. "Next year there will be no more refining capacity and we see consumption continuing to grow, and the only way to meet demand is to draw down stock levels," Brain said.

Lead is already in much better shape as stocks peaked at only twice their normal levels. "By the end of this year, we will be at or below normal levels," Brain said. Normal was defined as four weeks' supply throughout the system. Lead stocks were set to shrink 150,000 tonnes this year.

The lead stock drop will support firm lead prices whose normal levels are about 35 cents per pound. "The fundamentals support the current lead price and may exert a little upward pressure on it," Brain said.

Although lead was becoming a one market commodity, serving the batterymaking industry, demand for batteries looked good. "The battery business continues to grow and lead fundamentals look quite good for the next few years," Brain said.

This year, Cominco's Cajamarquilla smelter in Peru will exceed nameplate capacity and produce over 100,000 tonnes of zinc, a record for the plant. No decision has been taken on whether to expand to 230,000 tonnes of zinc a year.

Cominco's new 120,000 tonnes per year Kivcet lead plant in Trail will start up in early 1997, replacing an aging 100,000 tonne plant. Zinc metal production at Trail also rises next year to 290,000 tonnes, up 20,000 tonnes from 1996 levels.
